title: The Gaps To Fill in Supporting Faculty & Staff with Generative AI
author: Lance Eaton
summary: Lance Eaton reflects on why he is so often asked to speak to faculty about generative AI and what he actually brings to those rooms. He names six contributions: clarity that cuts through hype, simple frameworks for locating oneself, validation of faculty work, honesty about difficulty, centering the audience, and light-heartedness. The central move is to treat AI adoption as a people problem that is solved the way good teaching is, by listening to and respecting the learners rather than lecturing at them. He argues institutional leaders go wrong when they cast skeptical faculty as luddites. The piece ends by inviting readers to add what else effective AI facilitators bring.
points: Treating skeptical faculty as luddites creates as many problems as the technology itself, so validation of their prior adaptations must come first.
A simple framework, such as four stances from leaning in to leaning away, helps people name where they are before deciding what to do next.
Honest facilitators admit uncertainty and say I do not know, because no oracle of AI will save institutions.
Effective AI sessions end by centering the room, since the wisdom is in the faculty and staff who must learn from one another.
Levity is a legitimate tool for lowering the tension that the scale of the AI change creates.
quotes: Sifting through it all is impossible. Therefore, I offer a space to discuss it in layman’s terms and ground folks about what it is and isn’t. As important, I can often frame how generative AI might be relevant to one’s domain is important.

A mistake I see a lot of institutional leaders doing in this work is to assume that skeptical faculty are luddites or just not wanting to do the work. This assumption is likely to create as many problems as generative AI is for faculty because it fails to understand or listen to what’s really going on for many faculty.

Faculty and staff are not ignorant nor lacking precedence for skepticism—they’ve lived through how all the great technologies from the computer to Web 2.0 to MOOCs and the like were going to revolutionize education. And while changes have occurred, they’re far from the promised revolutions and often required as much work as faculty were already doing.
But I’m a drop of water and they are the water-filled bucket. So, I tell them that. The wisdom is in the room and they need to look and learn from one another about what they’re already doing.

We bring a very human element to what feels like a very inhuman and big challenge. We do the thing that I think great educators the world round do—we connect with the values and experiences of our learners and use that to build pathways for folks to step into a world that still may feel very much beyond what they were ready.
